Linux and macOS workstation login and privilege elevation

17 scenarios: LLOG01–05, LELEV01–04, MLOG01–05 and MELEV01–03. This is a worker implementation plan against the accepted corrections2/source baseline; it is not a report of executed Linux/macOS integration tests.

Product placement and boundaries

Use the dedicated Workstations workspace with Windows, Linux and macOS sign-in and elevation/local-authorization families. Keep LSM enforcement as a topic inside local authorization. SSH remains in its existing remote-access group, linked from relevant logon lessons; its network authentication must not be reimplemented here. SMB/NFS remain resource-access continuations.

Use a shared explanation panel for identity lookup → authentication → admission/authorization → session or operation, but do not force all systems into an identical execution order. Always display three distinct identities when relevant: requester, authenticated identity, and execution target. Local UID/account, realm principal, directory object and IdP subject can be related without being identical.

Reference profiles and evidence requirements

The source snapshot date is 2026-10-21. Source metadata below records observed publication/version information. Live pages are not immutable release pins. Before implementation sign-off, freeze each used source with resolved URL, retrieved date, title, section, revision/commit when available, and content hash. Record actual OS/build, packages, hardware, PAM stack, NSS configuration, SSSD provider, access policy and cache settings for every empirical claim.

Linux profiles are explicit compositions, not a fictitious universal Linux distribution. The reference systemd page identifies version 262; that does not establish the version shipped by any selected distribution. Use a reproducible vendor-supported machine image for native evidence and its installed manuals/configuration. RHEL 9 offline-cache documentation is a named provider profile, not a claim that all providers share its defaults. SELinux and AppArmor require separate loaded-policy fixtures.

Apple documentation observed here includes macOS 27 capability gates. Pin the selected OS and extension and distinguish support from deployment configuration. Keep Apple silicon/T2 FileVault behavior separate from unsupported hardware generalizations. Archived Authorization Services documentation supports conceptual rights boundaries only; it does not justify implementing deprecated privileged-execution APIs. Apple OSS main code is not automatically the source of the installed macOS binary.

Shared implementation contract

  • Represent PAM auth, account, password and session calls separately. NSS obtains identities; it does not prove a password. pam_systemd registers/manages a session where configured. LSM means Linux Security Modules and enforces access policy; it is not a network logon protocol.
  • Use local-event rendering for PAM calls, sudo policy checks, biometric decisions, keychain operations and kernel checks. Only actual sourced network exchanges get wire-message semantics. Do not invent undocumented Apple wire formats.
  • Keep offline cached verifier, retained TGT, newly issued TGT, sudo timestamp, polkit temporary authorization, Apple authorization reference, secure token and bootstrap token as different object types, owners and lifetimes. No cache object silently transforms into another credential.
  • Each scenario has deterministic success/denial branches with phase-specific stop points. Receiving authentication success cannot bypass a later policy gate. Local sessions may survive a failed remote request; the denial must not erase unrelated pre-existing holdings.
  • Reuse accepted field replay and held-object contracts: registered local operation names, correct actor/read grants, visible creation/use/verification/eviction and source cursors. Keep configuration inspect-only; do not generate a replay action from descriptive policy prose.
  • Use existing Kerberos/AD/SSH/service models through explicit links or shared subflows. Standalone Kerberos AS/PKINIT/FAST is not duplicated here. Ordinary Linux or Mac login must not be advertised as always obtaining a TGT.
  • Provide a compact outcome panel: local identity, network identity, authenticated by, authorization decision, resulting session/operation, and retained credentials. In advanced view show the exact profile and reason the branch stopped.

Implementation and verification order

  1. Land the shared identity/admission/session data contract and LLOG01/MLOG01, with no platform-specific network assumptions.
  2. Add online/offline directory and explicit ticket boundaries; link existing Kerberos and resource-access lessons.
  3. Add sudo/su/polkit and Mac scoped authorization; exercise alternate authenticated/target identities and no-prompt policy branches.
  4. Add LSM, FileVault/token boundaries and managed Platform SSO methods with explicit support gates.
  5. Run focused model/held-object/replay tests and mounted usability checks. Native integration evidence should use isolated test machines, synthetic accounts and read-only observation where possible, with OS/package/config hashes. Missing platform access must be recorded as unverified, never converted into synthetic pass logs.

Acceptance evidence must include identity lookup success with authentication failure; authentication success with admission denial; offline success without a new TGT; policy denial despite cached authentication; non-root execution targets; root/no-password configuration; LSM denial after elevation; FileVault eligibility independent of administrator membership; and canceled/unsupported biometric approval. A network-only IdP administrator must fail secure-token/ownership-only operations.

Scenario specifications

LLOG01 — Linux local workstation login through PAM

Explain the local identity, authentication, account-policy and session boundaries using a declared PAM service stack.

Actors: Person; Console login or display-manager service; PAM stack; Local identity/credential database; Session manager/logind

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-PAM: one explicitly supplied service stack; local files identity and pam_unix password backend; no directory or KDC dependency.
  • Select systemd session integration explicitly; do not imply every Linux login uses logind or the same stack ordering.

Causal steps

  1. Resolve the entered local account to UID, GID, groups, home and shell; label this identity lookup rather than proof of identity.
  2. Start the named PAM transaction and show the conversation delivering a secret only to the selected authentication module.
  3. Evaluate configured auth-stack control flow and the credential verdict.
  4. Run account checks separately; make account expiry or access denial visible after successful authentication.
  5. Establish credentials and open the session in the application profile; show pam_systemd registration only where configured, then the resulting process identity.
  6. Close the session and PAM transaction; discard transient secret/conversation state while preserving the account record.

Negative branches

  • Unknown user; incorrect password; authenticated account denied; session setup failure.
  • A blank password is denied in the baseline. A nullok or passwordless account requires a separately labeled explicit configuration.

Acceptance

  • Auth success alone cannot create the desktop; account and session gates must be represented.
  • Held objects distinguish identity record, verifier, transient entered secret and session handle; the application never receives the stored password verifier as a reusable login token.
  • Local calls and filesystem accesses are not fake network packets. Basic and expert views use the same causal events.

Sources: UPAM, PAMAPI, PAMUNIX, LOGIND

LLOG02 — Linux online directory logon with SSSD and Kerberos

Show how a domain identity becomes an authorized Linux session without equating directory lookup, Kerberos proof and host admission.

Actors: Person; Login application/PAM; SSSD PAM and NSS responders; Directory and KDC; Linux session manager

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-SSSD-AD: explicitly configured AD provider, domain enrollment/machine keytab, DNS/time/reachability, ID mapping and one access-provider policy.
  • Use modern allowed Kerberos enctypes; share existing AD/Kerberos lessons for AS exchanges. An IPA variant must name HBAC and its own provider, not relabel AD GPO behavior.

Causal steps

  1. Resolve directory user/group data through NSS and SSSD; retain the mapped UID/GIDs separately from the realm principal.
  2. Pass the PAM authentication request to SSSD; obtain/validate the Kerberos result through the selected provider.
  3. Expose a user TGT and credential cache only after an actual successful AS exchange; keep machine-account credentials separate.
  4. Evaluate the configured SSSD account/access provider for this host and PAM service.
  5. Create the local process session, credentials, home/session resources under the chosen stack.
  6. Link the existing ticket to later service-access lessons without implying login grants those resource permissions.

Negative branches

  • Identity resolves but password fails; credentials succeed but host policy denies; missing UID mapping; KDC unavailable with cache disabled.

Acceptance

  • Separate NSS/PAM responders and LDAP identity versus Kerberos authentication in the trace.
  • Tests assert the denied account has no workstation session even when a TGT was obtained; ticket cleanup/retention follows the explicitly chosen provider policy.
  • Record access_provider, ID-mapping mode and ccache implementation in the profile; no universal SSSD ordering or Linux-domain default.

Sources: SSSD, SSSDNSS, SSSDAD, KINIT, UPAM

LLOG03 — Linux cached directory logon while offline

Demonstrate local verification of previously cached credentials and the limits of offline knowledge and tickets.

Actors: Person; Login/PAM; SSSD cache and offline provider state; Unreachable directory/KDC; Session manager

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-SSSD-CACHE: successful prior online password logon, cache_credentials enabled, explicit offline expiration/failure thresholds and retained identity/access data.
  • Baseline has no valid pre-existing TGT and does not retain plaintext credentials for deferred KDC acquisition.

Causal steps

  1. Show the prior online cache-population checkpoint and its age; do not mint a cache entry at first offline login.
  2. Determine provider offline state and read the cached identity.
  3. Check the entered password against the cached verifier and enforce selected local cache/failure policy.
  4. Apply the provider-specific cached account/access result; annotate that new central changes may be unknown offline.
  5. Open a local session on success while the Kerberos cache remains empty.
  6. Reconnect in a separate event; fresh directory/KDC authentication is required before presenting a newly issued TGT.

Negative branches

  • First-ever offline login; cache disabled or expired; wrong cached password; remote password changed after the last cache refresh.
  • Central revocation is not depicted as instantly received while disconnected.

Acceptance

  • No AS-REP or fresh TGT appears in the offline branch; any retained unexpired ticket must be a separately declared initial object.
  • The cache verifier is not a plaintext password, TGT or network bearer credential.
  • Do not conflate offline caching with SSSD cached_auth_timeout optimization while online. Evidence must identify the selected provider and actual config.

Sources: SSSDCACHE, SSSDNSS, KINIT

LLOG04 — Linux expired password and PAM token change

Explain why a correct old password can require a password-management step before login succeeds.

Actors: Person; Login application/PAM; Selected password module; Credential authority; Session manager

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-PAM-CHANGE uses a local pam_unix account with an expired authentication token; a separately sourced SSSD branch may target the directory.
  • Choose an application that supports token change; do not promise every PAM consumer can handle it.

Causal steps

  1. Authenticate the existing credential.
  2. Return the account result requiring a new authentication token.
  3. Run the configured password stack and distinguish preliminary checks from update.
  4. Ask for the new secret; evaluate the configured policy and update the correct authority.
  5. Continue only after successful change and remaining admission checks, then create the session.
  6. Release old/new plaintext secret objects; retain only the updated authority state and authorized session.

Negative branches

  • New password fails policy; current credential wrong; write/update fails; application cannot perform token change; directory authority unreachable in the directory branch.

Acceptance

  • A failed password update cannot appear as a successful login or update a different credential store.
  • The UI separates account expiry from password expiry; local and directory updates are explicit profile branches.
  • No browser OAuth token or network PAKE exchange is invented for an ordinary local PAM call.

Sources: UPAM, PAMAPI, PAMUNIX

LLOG05 — Nonjoined Linux workstation: local login then explicit Kerberos

Separate the local desktop account from an explicitly selected domain principal used for network access.

Actors: Local user/process; kinit and user credential cache; Realm KDC; Selected remote service

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-KINIT: an already established local session on a machine with no domain machine account; reachable realm, DNS/time and user credentials.
  • Use the existing Kerberos acquisition model. Cross-link accepted SMB lab-smb-nonjoined-kerberos as the conceptual network-access continuation, with a separately pinned Linux client profile if showing actual mount commands.

Causal steps

  1. Display local UID and the separately entered realm principal.
  2. Invoke kinit for that principal and link the existing AS/preauthentication flow.
  3. Store the successful TGT under the selected user-owned cache.
  4. Request a service ticket and enter the existing service authorization lesson.
  5. Remove/expire tickets while leaving the original local login unchanged.

Negative branches

  • Wrong realm credential or unreachable KDC; cache inaccessible; ticket expires; successful service authentication but remote ACL denies.

Acceptance

  • Obtaining a TGT never changes the local UID, creates domain enrollment or grants local administrator rights.
  • A domain identity cannot log into this OS solely because kinit works; local account resolution/admission needs separate configuration.
  • Do not duplicate SSH userauth or SMB packet models; provide links and a clear identity handoff.

Sources: KINIT, SSSDNSS, UPAM

LELEV01 — sudo: policy, authenticated identity and timestamp reuse

Show who is requesting, whose identity is checked and which account executes the requested command.

Actors: Caller process/person; sudo and sudoers policy; PAM/authentication provider; Timestamp store; Target command process

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-SUDO: explicit sudoers rule, command/arguments, requested Runas user/group and timestamp_type/timeout; select a PAM-enabled sudo build.
  • Baseline authenticates the caller. Named alternatives rootpw, targetpw and runaspw must display the actual authenticated account.

Causal steps

  1. Capture caller UID, requested command and target identity; evaluate sudoers authorization.
  2. Determine authentication requirement from matching rule and valid timestamp scope.
  3. If required, run the configured PAM authentication for the selected identity; include account/session effects where configured.
  4. Write or refresh only the appropriate timestamp record after successful authentication.
  5. Execute the allowed command with the target credentials and filtered environment; keep the invoking shell unchanged.
  6. Repeat within scope, after expiry and after invalidation to show when a prompt reappears.

Negative branches

  • Command/Runas denied despite correct password or valid timestamp; wrong password; expired or different-terminal timestamp; noninteractive invocation needs authentication.

Acceptance

  • Timestamp caching is authentication reuse, not a saved password or blanket grant of commands. Policy is checked on each request.
  • Explicit NOPASSWD/root-invocation branches can omit the password while retaining applicable policy/account/session checks. Do not call NOPASSWD a successful password comparison.
  • Target can be a non-root account; rootpw/targetpw/runaspw are selectable configuration differences, not silent defaults.

Sources: SUDO, SUDORENDER, SUDOTS, PAMAPI

LELEV02 — su and configured root bypass

Contrast substitute-user authentication with sudo delegation, including policy-driven passwordless root use.

Actors: Invoking user/process; util-linux su; PAM service stack; Target account backend; Target shell/process

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-SU: util-linux implementation, exact su/su-l PAM stack and target account; default demonstration uses a non-root caller and target password.
  • A root bypass requires an explicit configured pam_rootok rule; show real UID, not merely effective setuid authority.

Causal steps

  1. Select the target account and resolve its UID/groups/home/shell.
  2. Start su PAM processing and check the selected target credential unless the declared stack permits a bypass.
  3. Evaluate account/access rules even when no password prompt occurs, as the configured stack requires.
  4. Establish target process identity and the selected login-shell environment behavior.
  5. Return to the original caller after process termination and release transaction state.

Negative branches

  • Target password wrong or locked; wheel/access rule denies; missing target account; rootok does not accept an ordinary caller just because su itself is setuid-root.

Acceptance

  • No sudoers timestamp or command delegation is silently reused.
  • su --login environment setup is not presented as a complete new systemd-logind workstation entry session.
  • Link runuser for already privileged automation as an explanatory comparison, not a duplicated full scenario.

Sources: SU, PAMROOT, PAMAPI

LELEV03 — polkit: authorize one privileged operation

Explain a service authorization decision, its optional authentication challenge and the service action that follows.

Actors: Unprivileged client/subject; Privileged service/mechanism; polkit authority; Session authentication agent/helper; Credential provider

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-POLKIT: one real action ID, action details and pinned policy; declare local/active session and available agent.
  • Use an example such as a managed service or power operation only after documenting its actual action and policy.

Causal steps

  1. Client requests an operation from the privileged mechanism.
  2. Mechanism asks polkit about the subject and exact action.
  3. Return deny, allow, auth_self or auth_admin according to explicit policy.
  4. For a challenge, the agent authenticates an allowed identity through the native backend and reports the result through the privileged path.
  5. Authority completes the authorization decision; mechanism alone performs the allowed operation.
  6. For *_KEEP, show temporary authorization and its expiration/reuse scope; retain no universal root credential.

Negative branches

  • Authentication canceled/failed; no usable agent; policy denies; authenticated identity outside permitted administrator set; changed action or expired authorization.

Acceptance

  • Successful agent authentication alone cannot authorize an unrelated action or elevate the client process.
  • Test active/inactive and remote/no-agent branches against declared rules, without assuming all local users may perform the action.
  • When action-detail-dependent policy is demonstrated, do not use *_KEEP as though its built-in cache rechecks all those details.

Sources: POLKIT, POLKITAGENT

LELEV04 — LSM enforcement after login or elevation

Correct the LSM terminology and show why authenticated or elevated processes can still be denied resource access.

Actors: Already authenticated process; Kernel access checks; SELinux policy or AppArmor profile; Resource; Audit record

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile L-LSM-SELINUX or L-LSM-APPARMOR, each with an explicit loaded enforcing policy and concrete process/resource context.
  • These are separate system profiles of one lesson, not interchangeable rule syntaxes; no invented LSM login handshake.

Causal steps

  1. Carry a process identity from workstation login or sudo and show the requested file/action.
  2. Display the relevant ordinary access/capability conditions and mandatory policy inputs.
  3. For SELinux, evaluate the declared context/type rule; for AppArmor, evaluate the loaded task profile and applicable mediation rule.
  4. Deny the operation and produce a labeled policy/audit result without undoing authentication.
  5. Compare an explicitly permitted request or an unconfined profile as a declared policy alternative.

Negative branches

  • UID 0 remains denied under the chosen enforcing confinement; changed resource label/profile rule; no loaded profile must not be depicted as enforcing that profile.

Acceptance

  • LSM expands to Linux Security Modules and is authorization/enforcement, not a password protocol or PAM replacement.
  • Model policy inputs/result, not a universal fixed kernel-hook order.
  • No mandatory claim that every sudo operation changes SELinux domain or AppArmor profile; transitions require explicit policy evidence.

Sources: LSM, APPARMOR, SELINUX

MLOG01 — Mac local login, screen unlock and local identity

Establish the local-account boundary before directory SSO and privileged-operation lessons.

Actors: Person; Login window or lock screen; Local account/authentication service; User session; Optional Touch ID hardware

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile M-LOCAL: existing local user, FileVault already unlocked or deliberately excluded from this trace; no Platform SSO requirement.
  • Select a supported hardware/OS profile for Touch ID. Initial login and unlocking an existing session are distinct entry states.

Causal steps

  1. Identify the local account and present the appropriate login or unlock prompt.
  2. Validate the local credential using an opaque OS operation, without asserting undocumented hash/wire details.
  3. Create a user session or unlock the existing one, preserving the selected identity.
  4. In the optional supported Touch ID unlock branch, show local biometric verification and the resulting local decision.
  5. Require the password when the chosen documented state disallows biometrics, including startup; release transient authentication state.

Negative branches

  • Wrong local password; unsupported or unavailable biometric method; required password cannot be replaced with an Apple Account password.

Acceptance

  • Local login, Apple Account sign-in, FileVault unlock and administrative approval remain separately named states.
  • No Kerberos TGT, OAuth token or administrator permission appears solely because a desktop opens.
  • The main trace remains useful without synthetic private Apple packet fields.

Sources: MACLOCAL, MACTOUCH

MLOG02 — Mac FileVault unlock, secure token and volume ownership

Show disk-key access before OS-session and administrator decisions, and distinguish the different Apple token concepts.

Actors: Person or recovery-key holder; Boot/unlock environment; Secure Enclave on selected hardware; Encrypted APFS volume; OS login service

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile M-FV: Apple silicon/T2 internal APFS with FileVault enabled and an explicitly eligible unlock account.
  • Show secure-token state, bootstrap-token escrow state and volume-owner status as separate initial properties; none is an OAuth bearer token.

Causal steps

  1. Start with encrypted data unavailable.
  2. Validate the selected unlock credential or explicitly chosen recovery method.
  3. Represent the protected key-unwrapping/decryption boundary without exposing Secure Enclave key bytes to the app or CPU.
  4. Make data volume access available; continue to the OS-session gate, acknowledging supported credential handoff can avoid a second visible prompt.
  5. Explain bootstrap-token provisioning/escrow and volume ownership in a linked state panel, not a fabricated user-login packet.

Negative branches

  • Wrong unlock credential; user not enabled for the selected unlock path; admin group membership alone insufficient; missing recovery material.

Acceptance

  • Disk unlocked does not by itself mean administrator action authorized or remote IdP authenticated.
  • A volume owner may be a standard user; tasks requiring both ownership and administrator rights need both predicates.
  • Record hardware, OS and provisioning path. The documented macOS 26+ enrollment bootstrap-token path must not be replaced by an older universal first-login-only story.

Sources: MACFV, MACTOKENS

MLOG03 — Mac AD network/mobile account: online and cached login

Cover bound-directory workstation login and its explicitly configured offline mobile-account variant.

Actors: Person; Login window and directory services; AD connector/local mobile-account cache; AD directory/KDC; Local session

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile M-AD: supported macOS build, bound AD connector, modern permitted Kerberos settings and explicit mobile-account creation choice.
  • Offline branch requires an existing mobile account populated by prior online login; a network-only account is not automatically an offline account.

Causal steps

  1. Resolve account and groups through the directory connector.
  2. Online: use the selected Kerberos authentication path and evaluate the relevant directory/local account policy.
  3. If configured, create/update the mobile account cache and create the local user session.
  4. Offline continuation: use the existing mobile-account credential state and clearly mark central authorities unreachable.
  5. Show newly obtained tickets only in an online exchange; link an available ticket to existing service-access lessons.
  6. Separate directory password change, cached password and login-keychain state when demonstrating resynchronization.

Negative branches

  • No cached mobile account while offline; incorrect cache credential; online KDC failure; password changed elsewhere; authenticated user denied local admission.

Acceptance

  • Do not show a fresh TGT emitted by an offline credential check.
  • Directory identity resolution and Kerberos authentication remain different steps; do not describe LDAP lookup as password proof.
  • No legacy AD functional-level or weak-crypto example becomes the new default.

Sources: MACAD, MACMOBILE, KINIT

MLOG04 — Mac local account with Kerberos SSO extension

Demonstrate domain resource SSO without AD binding or a directory-backed workstation account.

Actors: Local user/session; Apple Kerberos SSO extension; AD KDC; User ticket cache; Kerberos-enabled resource

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile M-KERB-SSO: local Mac account, configured managed Kerberos SSO extension, reachable on-premises AD and explicit user authentication.
  • Any local-password synchronization is a selected policy feature; it does not make the local account an AD computer join.

Causal steps

  1. Begin in the existing local session.
  2. Trigger extension authentication on configured network/profile/user events.
  3. Perform the existing Kerberos acquisition flow and record a TGT only after KDC success.
  4. Use the ticket cache for a supported service and link the separate resource authorization step.
  5. Show renewal/reacquisition versus sign-out/expiration, without changing the local UID.

Negative branches

  • Local login works but AD unreachable; wrong domain credentials; expired ticket; service ACL denies; local and domain passwords diverge.

Acceptance

  • Explicitly state no AD binding/mobile login is required for this profile.
  • If combined with Platform SSO, select compatible domains/settings and avoid competing password synchronization.
  • Do not imply all applications or every username prompt automatically use the extension.

Sources: MACKRB, MACPSSO, KINIT

MLOG05 — Mac Platform SSO: registration, login policy and IdP identity

Explain managed Platform SSO without treating local login, IdP authentication and account privilege as one token exchange.

Actors: Person; Mac local authentication/Platform SSO; Configured SSO extension; Identity provider; Device management service

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile M-PSSO: pin macOS version, IdP/extension version and exact configuration. Baseline covers password and Secure Enclave key methods as alternative branches.
  • State device registration, user registration and local-account creation status; capture configured offline/login policy.

Causal steps

  1. Show device and user registration dependencies and the established local-account association.
  2. Select the configured method and login policy; show local password handling separately from IdP proof.
  3. Password method: apply the configured online requirement/offline allowance and password synchronization outcome.
  4. Secure Enclave key method: retain the local-password login boundary and show a separate hardware-key IdP authentication operation.
  5. Record the resulting local session and separate IdP SSO state, then link application-token use.
  6. Expose version-specific optional methods only when the extension and current Apple capability table support them.

Negative branches

  • Registration incomplete; IdP unreachable under required-online policy; unsupported method; failed remote proof; disabled/exempt account mismatch.

Acceptance

  • Do not draw proprietary IdP messages without that provider specification and captured version.
  • Required-online and offline-grace branches must be causally different.
  • Gate newer web/QR/required-Touch-ID behavior to documented macOS 27 support; earlier availability of Platform SSO alone is insufficient.

Sources: MACPSSO, MACTOKENS, MACLOCAL

MELEV01 — Mac administrator authorization for a scoped GUI operation

Explain operation-specific authorization without turning the whole desktop or application into root.

Actors: Requesting user/app; OS authorization service and prompt; Permitted administrator identity; Privileged service/helper; Protected operation

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile M-AUTHZ: one supported privileged operation and its actual authorization right/policy; local administrator baseline.
  • This models OS behavior; do not implement a native privileged helper or use deprecated AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges.

Causal steps

  1. Request a named operation and its authorization right.
  2. Evaluate the right and decide whether an eligible administrator must authenticate.
  3. Obtain an allowed administrator identity, which may differ from the logged-in user.
  4. Validate required authentication and grant only the operation/right scope defined by policy.
  5. Privileged component verifies authorization and performs the operation; client identity remains unchanged.
  6. Release the authorization reference or show bounded reuse only where the chosen right permits it.

Negative branches

  • Correct standard-user password insufficient; prompt canceled; right denied; different operation not covered; stale or invalid authorization.

Acceptance

  • Separate requester, authenticated administrator and executing service identities.
  • Optional Touch ID/Apple Watch approval appears only for a documented supported prompt and configured hardware/account state; no synthetic wireless protocol.
  • No global root token, secure token, TGT or FileVault entitlement is created by this approval.

Sources: MACADMIN, MACAUTH, MACAUTHTASKS, MACWATCH, MACMOBILE

MELEV02 — Mac sudo with password or configured Touch ID

Show macOS command elevation as sudo policy plus its actual PAM/authentication configuration.

Actors: Caller/Terminal; sudo policy and timestamp store; macOS PAM modules; Local authentication service; Target command

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile M-SUDO: record OS build, bundled sudo version and effective /etc/pam.d/sudo include chain.
  • Password baseline; Touch ID is an explicit supported/configured branch using Apple pam_tid, not assumed enabled everywhere.

Causal steps

  1. Choose caller, command and target identity; evaluate sudo authorization.
  2. Check timestamp scope and whether fresh authentication is needed.
  3. Password branch invokes its configured provider; Touch ID branch identifies the PAM user and asks the local system for the permitted verification.
  4. Accept the method result only through the selected stack; fallback is explicit stack behavior.
  5. Run the allowed command with target credentials and retain the invoking desktop identity.
  6. Expire/invalidate authentication reuse and clean up transient state.

Negative branches

  • Policy denies despite biometric success; no eligible local UI/session; canceled or failed verification; unsupported module/configuration; timestamp expires.

Acceptance

  • Reuse LELEV01 policy/timestamp concepts while retaining an independent macOS implementation profile.
  • Apple OSS main is evidence of module behavior, not proof of the exact shipping build or local configuration.
  • Do not promise Touch ID for SSH/headless sessions or every sudo configuration; do not map Apple Watch GUI support automatically onto sudo.

Sources: SUDO, SUDOTS, MACTID, MACTOUCH

MELEV03 — Mac Platform SSO network administrator authorization

Show the distinct case where an IdP identity without a local account can authorize a supported administrator prompt.

Actors: Local requesting app/user; Platform SSO and authorization service; Network-only IdP administrator; IdP/extension; Privileged operation

Profile and preconditions

  • Profile M-PSSO-NETADMIN: supported macOS/extension, shared device keys and explicitly configured administrator/group mappings.
  • Choose an operation eligible for network authorization; it must not require secure token, volume ownership or authentication specifically by the current local user.

Causal steps

  1. Start a supported authorization request under an existing local session.
  2. Select the allowed network-only identity and authenticate through the configured provider.
  3. Evaluate the returned group/privilege mapping and requested right.
  4. Grant the scoped authorization and perform the operation without creating a local user merely to label the network identity.
  5. Compare a secure-token/ownership-specific operation, which must select a different eligible authorization path or fail.

Negative branches

  • IdP unavailable; administrator group mapping absent; network identity authentication succeeds but right denied; operation requires excluded local/ownership credentials.

Acceptance

  • Network-only administrator proof does not manufacture a secure token, volume ownership or a workstation login session.
  • Keep the IdP mapping policy inspectable and show only the documented provider exchange.
  • This is a separate authorization capability from ordinary Platform SSO login, not a renamed local-administrator scenario.

Sources: MACPSSO, MACAUTH, MACTOKENS
