JWT foundations and dedicated Kubernetes group

Worker scope: 9 JWT scenarios and 16 Kubernetes scenarios, with K8S16 as an optional extension family. The embedded scenario ledger and configuration bundles below are the structured specification; the contracts below are implementation acceptance requirements.

Version and feature profile

v1.37.1; confirmed published stable patch through official release page and release tag; not a claim that it is the newest available patch

The release page lists v1.37.2 with a 2026-10-13 target under Upcoming Patch. A passed target date is not proof of release. Before implementation freeze, record tag/commit or image digest and source revision; do not silently change this profile.

  • AuthenticationConfiguration and configurable anonymous endpoints: stable since v1.34.
  • client-go exec credential plugins: stable since v1.22; use ExecCredential v1.
  • ValidatingAdmissionPolicy: stable since v1.30; K8S08 uses admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1.
  • AuthorizationConfiguration: stable since v1.32.
  • ServiceAccount token volume projection: stable since v1.20; bound-token default volume mechanism: stable since v1.22. Keep these distinct feature names.
  • SelfSubjectReview: stable since v1.28.
  • Constrained impersonation: beta since v1.36, enabled by default in current docs; label and record gate state separately.
  • StructuredAuthenticationConfigurationEgressSelector is beta in current docs; not needed by default demo.
  • APIServerWebhookAuthenticationToken is alpha in v1.37; excluded from default profile.

Source discrepancies to keep visible

  • Authentication page repeats --oidc-signing-algs with inconsistent default values (RS256 in its OIDC table and RS512 later). Do not rely on either prose default: explicit RS256 for an optional flag-only profile and pinned-source verification. AuthenticationConfiguration v1 has no signingAlgs field; do not invent one.
  • Current documentation is moving. Archive consulted sections or tag the implementation evidence. Distinguish chosen teaching policy from Kubernetes implementation defaults.

Release evidence: official release record; published v1.37.1 tag. Research date: 2026-10-21.

Navigation and fixture

Create a dedicated Kubernetes group. Families: Human access; Token validation; Authorization and RBAC; Workload identity; Delegation and extensions. JWT foundations are a family under Foundations, linked from Web, Kubernetes and MCP.

Synthetic nonproduction demo, default authorizer chain Node,RBAC; Node has no opinion for these human/workload requests; no AlwaysAllow. Real-cluster validation, if added, must be isolated and version-pinned.

Namespaces: demo-dev, demo-prod. Alice maps to oidc:alice, group team:readers. Bob maps to oidc:bob, group team:observers. The reader Role permits only pod get/list/watch in demo-dev, bound to Alice’s group. Bob starts denied. ServiceAccount demo-dev/reader receives its own explicit grant only in the workload success fixture.

Human issuer https://issuer.demo.example; OIDC client/audience kubernetes-demo. Cluster token issuer/API audience https://kubernetes.demo.example; external workload audience vault.demo.example. These are illustrative nonproduction values.

Exact example policy and authentication configuration
{
  "role": {
    "apiVersion": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "Role",
    "metadata": {
      "name": "reader",
      "namespace": "demo-dev"
    },
    "rules": [
      {
        "apiGroups": [
          ""
        ],
        "resources": [
          "pods"
        ],
        "verbs": [
          "get",
          "list",
          "watch"
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  "roleBinding": {
    "apiVersion": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "RoleBinding",
    "metadata": {
      "name": "read-pods",
      "namespace": "demo-dev"
    },
    "subjects": [
      {
        "kind": "Group",
        "name": "team:readers",
        "apiGroup": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
      }
    ],
    "roleRef": {
      "kind": "Role",
      "name": "reader",
      "apiGroup": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
    }
  },
  "authenticationConfigExample": {
    "apiVersion": "apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "AuthenticationConfiguration",
    "anonymous": {
      "enabled": false
    },
    "jwt": [
      {
        "issuer": {
          "url": "https://issuer.demo.example",
          "audiences": [
            "kubernetes-demo"
          ],
          "audienceMatchPolicy": "MatchAny"
        },
        "claimValidationRules": [
          {
            "claim": "tenant",
            "requiredValue": "demo"
          }
        ],
        "claimMappings": {
          "username": {
            "claim": "sub",
            "prefix": "oidc:"
          },
          "groups": {
            "claim": "groups",
            "prefix": "team:"
          }
        },
        "userValidationRules": [
          {
            "expression": "!user.username.startsWith('system:')",
            "message": "human username must not use a system prefix"
          },
          {
            "expression": "user.groups.all(group, !group.startsWith('system:'))",
            "message": "mapped human groups must not use a system prefix"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

API server adds system:authenticated after external mapping; validation example constrains mapped issuer groups. Worker must validate exact v1 schema and evaluation order against selected tag before presenting runnable YAML. No --oidc-* arguments may be combined with --authentication-config.

Shared implementation and review requirements

  • Create a dedicated Kubernetes navigation/workspace group with Human access, Token validation, Authorization/RBAC, Workload identity, and Delegation/extensions families. JWT foundations are their own shared family linked from K8s and existing OAuth/OIDC/JWE lessons. Do not bury Kubernetes inside generic OAuth or silently duplicate existing lessons.
  • Use canonical events, explicit actor-local holdings and immutable artifact/generation IDs. Track received bytes, parsed untrusted claims, verified signature, validated claims, mapped userInfo, authorization input/verdict, admission proposal/verdict, persisted object and response separately. Reading a claim never creates permission.
  • Model API authentication/RBAC/admission as local API-server stages; different swimlanes may explain responsibilities but must not fabricate network hops. The API server may read from watch caches; a symbolic storage boundary must not imply every read makes a new etcd network RPC.
  • Each scenario has a fixed happy path and independently selectable failures with declared policy. Branches must alter the relevant request/claim/key/rule/state, not only the narration. Do not silently recover into another authenticator or grant.
  • JWT validation requires primary-source rules and profile-specific requirements. Public key retrieval is not proof of trust by itself. Never expose issuer private keys, refresh tokens or plaintext JWE contents to actors that do not possess them. Bearer token display is synthetic and clearly labeled.
  • Maintain overview/field/exact-object replay parity. Exact history must retain token envelope versus decrypted/validated representation, principal origin, binding rule and namespace; backwards seek must rebuild state deterministically and clear stale grants/results.
  • Provide a visible decision strip: credential → identity → requested action → matching grant → admission when relevant → result. Show why a step is skipped. Error cards name failing stage, caller identity, actual status and next meaningful action; do not map all 403s to RBAC.
  • Navigation, source/profile expanders and scenario switches need keyboard focus return, readable 390px layout, no token overflow, accessible branch labels and no color-only success signal. Keep five or fewer actors horizontally; break browser/login and API authorization into linked phases without losing artifacts.
  • Source panel pins release/profile/feature maturity, RFC section or Kubernetes section, retrieval date, implementation-specific cache policy and limits. Mark symbolic fixtures as symbolic; cryptographic validity requires separately computed test vectors rather than decorative signatures.
  • Tests should prove state boundaries and failure behavior, not mirror prose. Test route registration, all declared scenario IDs, preservation of existing OIDC/JWT/JWE paths, policy reset, identity mapping, exact-request RBAC decisions, JWT/key/token rotation, representation custody, no post-rejection persistence, and actual mounted field-to-exact-history transitions.
  • Before claiming runnable Kubernetes conformance, validate config/manifests and critical status/feature behavior against pinned v1.37.1 executable or source. Native-browser evidence remains separate from DOM tests and from live Kubernetes interoperability. Report any source discrepancy instead of inventing a consensus.

Scenario contracts

JWT01 — JWT, JWS, JWE and opaque tokens

Separate token representation from the protocol, protection and authorization decision.

Actors: Issuer; Client; Resource server

Preconditions

  • Three fixed synthetic examples; no real credentials; compact serialization explicitly selected.
  1. issue: Create a signed three-segment JWT, encrypted five-segment JWT, and opaque reference token. Held state: Issuer owns source claims; each output has its own exact artifact ID.
  2. inspect: Let the holder decode JWS header/payload, inspect JWE envelope only, and view opaque bytes only. Held state: Decoded JWS claims remain unverified; JWE plaintext is absent at holders without the decryption key.
  3. validate: Route each artifact to its configured validation path. Held state: Parsing creates no authenticated identity or access grant.
  4. compare: Show protection and validator panels side by side. Held state: JWT is a claims format; JWS gives integrity, JWE confidentiality/integrity; opaque is a client representation, not inherently weaker.

Negative cases

  • Malformed segment/base64url/JSON input produces a parse error before trust state.
  • Do not infer token format merely from an OAuth response field name.

Acceptance

  • Inspection never labels base64url decoding as decryption.
  • Do not state that every JWS is a JWT, every JWT is encrypted, or JWT itself is an authentication protocol.

Sources: RFC 7519 (3; 4.1; 5; 7; 11); RFC 7515 (3.1; 4; 5; 10); RFC 7516 (3.1; 4; 5; 11); RFC 7662 (2; 4)

JWT02 — Signed JWT verification and tampering

Show exactly what signature verification establishes and what still needs checking.

Actors: Issuer; Bearer client; API verifier

Preconditions

  • RS256 demo profile with a pinned trusted issuer key; source bytes and encoded signing input retained.
  1. issue: Issuer signs BASE64URL(header).BASE64URL(payload). Held state: Private signing key remains at issuer; public verification key is verifier-local.
  2. receive: API receives the exact compact token over the selected TLS carrier. Held state: Inbox holds received bytes and untrusted decoded claims.
  3. verify: Verify signature with configured key and algorithm. Held state: A local signature-valid observation references the same token generation.
  4. validate: Run issuer/audience/time/profile checks before policy. Held state: Only all-success creates validatedClaims; access still requires separate policy.

Negative cases

  • Flip one payload byte or signature byte: verification fails.
  • A correctly signed token for another API must still fail contextual validation.

Acceptance

  • No private key is delivered to client or verifier.
  • Failure creates no accepted identity; exact-history shows receive, parse, verify and claim acceptance separately.

Sources: RFC 7515 (3.1; 4; 5; 10); RFC 7519 (3; 4.1; 5; 7; 11); RFC 8725 / BCP 225 (2; 3.1-3.12)

JWT03 — Encrypted and nested JWT acceptance

Explain decryption, AEAD validation and inner signature validation as distinct steps.

Actors: Signing issuer; Encryption recipient; Carrier client

Preconditions

  • Explicit sign-then-encrypt profile; outer alg RSA-OAEP-256 and enc A128GCM; inner signed JWT; cty JWT.
  1. nest: Create inner signed JWT, then encrypt it to the recipient public key. Held state: Issuer keeps signing secret; recipient alone holds private decryption key; CEK has explicit local custody.
  2. receive: Deliver JWE compact envelope. Held state: Carrier and recipient inbox inspect ciphertext; no automatically acquired plaintext.
  3. unwrap: Validate encryption parameters and authentication tag, then expose inner bytes locally. Held state: Authenticated decryption creates recipient-local inner JWS; claims still lack issuer acceptance.
  4. accept: Verify inner signature and expected JWT profile claims. Held state: Separate decrypt-valid, signature-valid and claims-valid observations precede use.

Negative cases

  • Wrong recipient key or changed tag produces no plaintext acquisition.
  • Valid outer JWE with invalid inner signature is rejected; encryption alone does not prove sender identity.

Acceptance

  • Never perform encrypt-then-skip-signature acceptance.
  • Clarify compact segment counts are serialization-specific; JWE is not the Kubernetes human-token profile.

Sources: RFC 7516 (3.1; 4; 5; 11); RFC 7519 (3; 4.1; 5; 7; 11); RFC 8725 / BCP 225 (2; 3.1-3.12)

JWT04 — Algorithm and key-type confusion rejected

Make algorithm policy an input to verification, not a value chosen by the attacker.

Actors: Issuer; Verifier

Preconditions

  • Demo verifier allowlist RS256 only; keys bound to algorithm and purpose; no unsigned-token use case.
  1. configure: Install trusted algorithm/key profile before token arrival. Held state: Verifier owns immutable profile revision.
  2. receive: Read untrusted alg header and candidate key metadata. Held state: Header is a hint, not authorization to select any primitive.
  3. check: Reject none, unexpected HS256, key-type mismatch or incompatible use/key_ops. Held state: Failure references the rejecting constraint before any trusted-claims state.
  4. verify: Allow matching RS256 candidate through cryptographic verification and contextual checks. Held state: Only successful checks create acceptance.

Negative cases

  • RSA public bytes must never become an HMAC shared secret.
  • Unknown critical header extension is rejected if the profile cannot process it.

Acceptance

  • Selected algorithm and allowlist visible together; no silent downgrade.
  • Do not imply RFC 7519 universally bans unsecured JWTs; this accepting profile explicitly does.

Sources: RFC 8725 / BCP 225 (2; 3.1-3.12); RFC 7515 (3.1; 4; 5; 10); RFC 7517 (4.2-4.5; 5; 9)

JWT05 — Issuer trust, discovery, kid and JWKS

Explain where trusted verification keys come from and what kid does not prove.

Actors: Configured verifier; Issuer discovery endpoint; JWKS endpoint; Token presenter

Preconditions

  • Fixed issuer https://issuer.demo.example; HTTPS trust; issuer-scoped JWKS cache; asymmetric public keys only.
  1. discover: Fetch configured issuer metadata and check returned issuer equals expected issuer. Held state: Verifier stores a validated metadata revision and trusted jwks_uri.
  2. fetch: Retrieve JWKS from that trusted URI. Held state: Verifier caches public verification candidates; issuer private keys never leave issuer.
  3. select: Use kid as an untrusted selector within this issuer key set; filter type, purpose and algorithm. Held state: Candidate selection is distinct from signature verification.
  4. accept: Verify the token and profile before adopting claims. Held state: Verified issuer/key reference accompanies accepted token.

Negative cases

  • A token-supplied jku/x5u is not followed by this profile.
  • Unknown or ambiguous kid fails according to the declared profile, never falls back to arbitrary keys/issuers.

Acceptance

  • kid is not a key, globally unique identity or proof of trust.
  • JWKS response/cache and signature check appear as separate artifacts and local events.

Sources: OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0, errata set 2 (3; 4.3; 7); RFC 7517 (4.2-4.5; 5; 9); RFC 8725 / BCP 225 (2; 3.1-3.12)

JWT06 — JWKS rotation and bounded refresh

Teach availability and key rotation without inventing an RFC-mandated cache lifetime.

Actors: Issuer; JWKS server; Verifier cache; Client

Preconditions

  • Explicit demo policy: cache TTL 300s; one in-flight refresh per issuer; minimum 30s refresh interval; bounded negative cache; 2s fetch timeout; no stale-key acceptance after profile freshness limit. These are demo policies, not universal RFC/Kubernetes defaults.
  1. overlap: Publish old+new public keys before issuing tokens with new kid. Held state: Cache initially holds old key; issuer retains both signing generations during selected overlap.
  2. refresh: Receive new kid; if refresh budget allows, perform one coalesced JWKS refresh. Held state: Pending tokens stay unaccepted; requests share refresh work.
  3. verify: Find new key, verify token and claims, then accept. Held state: Cache revision and token key generation are explicit.
  4. retire: After declared lifetime/overlap, retire old key and expire cache entries. Held state: Retirement is not instantaneous universal token revocation.

Negative cases

  • Unknown-kid flood is rate/capacity bounded.
  • Refresh timeout/missing new kid denies that token; an unrelated valid cached-key token follows its own declared freshness policy.

Acceptance

  • Deterministic clock tests cover overlap, timeout and retry budget.
  • Kubernetes-specific refresh internals must be checked against pinned implementation before claiming identical timings.

Sources: RFC 7517 (4.2-4.5; 5; 9); OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0, errata set 2 (3; 4.3; 7); OpenID Connect Core 1.0, errata set 2 (2; 3.1.2; 3.1.3.7; 12; 16.15); RFC 8725 / BCP 225 (2; 3.1-3.12)

JWT07 — Issuer, audience, time and claim types

Show why a valid signature alone is insufficient.

Actors: Issuer; API validator; Policy engine

Preconditions

  • Fixed now; configured skew 30s; required iss/sub/aud/exp; demo additionally requires iat; nbf optional. NumericDate represented in seconds.
  1. verify: Finish signature verification before trusting claim values. Held state: Received/decoded claims retained as untrusted evidence.
  2. context: Match exact issuer and intended audience; accept aud string or array only as allowed by profile. Held state: Issuer/audience observations identify expected and actual values.
  3. time: Evaluate exp, nbf when present, and separately declared iat/max-age policy. Held state: Clock/skew inputs shown; iat is not itself an expiration time.
  4. types: Validate required strings/arrays/numbers and subject semantics; then build accepted identity. Held state: Invalid types cannot coerce into an accepted subject/group.

Negative cases

  • Wrong issuer/audience, expired/not-yet-valid, missing required claim, milliseconds mistaken for seconds, or string exp rejected.
  • Duplicate claim names are rejected by this stricter demo parser; do not claim every conforming JWT parser must choose that option.

Acceptance

  • Boundary tests use deterministic timestamps and profile-required vs optional badges.
  • No rule says all registered JWT claims are universally required.

Sources: RFC 7519 (3; 4.1; 5; 7; 11); RFC 8725 / BCP 225 (2; 3.1-3.12)

JWT08 — ID tokens, access tokens and cross-JWT substitution

Teach purpose-specific validation and the Kubernetes ID-token integration as a deliberate profile.

Actors: OIDC client; Issuer; Ordinary resource API; Kubernetes API profile

Preconditions

  • OIDC client audience demo-native; ordinary API audience https://api.demo.example; RFC9068 access-token typ at+jwt; separate validators.
  1. issue: Issue ID token for client authentication and access token for resource access. Held state: Different exact artifacts, audiences, lifetimes and intended consumers.
  2. client: Client validates ID token including transaction nonce when used. Held state: Client login state is distinct from API authorization.
  3. resource: Ordinary API applies RFC9068 type, issuer, audience and authorization profile. Held state: ID-token substitution fails this resource profile.
  4. kubernetes: Link to K8S01, whose configured OIDC integration deliberately sends an appropriate ID token as bearer credential. Held state: No inference that all APIs accept ID tokens, or every access token is a JWT.

Negative cases

  • Wrong-purpose token with a valid signature rejected using mutually exclusive profile rules.
  • A typ value alone never proves purpose; compare expected audience/issuer and required claims too.

Acceptance

  • Do not invent mandatory typ=id_token in OIDC Core or K8s.
  • Do not assert the API server universally distinguishes ID vs access tokens by their origin; show which actual configured check fails.

Sources: OpenID Connect Core 1.0, errata set 2 (2; 3.1.2; 3.1.3.7; 12; 16.15); RFC 9068 (2; 4); RFC 8725 / BCP 225 (2; 3.1-3.12); Kubernetes Authenticating: user-requested OIDC source (OIDC tokens; structured configuration; client-go credential plugins; anonymous requests)

JWT09 — Bearer possession, replay and validation lifetime

Separate token validity, proof of possession and current server-side status.

Actors: Holder; API; Introspection endpoint; Local JWT validator

Preconditions

  • Bearer profile over TLS; opaque-token comparison uses authenticated RFC7662 introspection; no DPoP/mTLS claim.
  1. present: Send same valid bearer token twice within validity interval. Held state: Each request obtains received credential; jti alone creates no replay cache.
  2. local: Local validator checks JWT with cached keys and context. Held state: No automatic revocation call or issuer session check occurs per request.
  3. introspect: For opaque comparison, API authenticates to introspection and evaluates active plus intended resource/profile. Held state: Introspection result has explicit cache TTL and evaluation time.
  4. expire: Advance clock or change introspection status; show differing rejection points. Held state: Rejected requests produce no new authorization grant; prior completed actions are not undone.

Negative cases

  • Do not present signing or JWE encryption as sender binding.
  • Introspection timeout follows declared fail-closed policy; cached results remain bounded by declared policy.

Acceptance

  • Logout does not imply immediate invalidation of every self-contained JWT.
  • Link existing sender-constrained flows if available instead of duplicating them; distinguish OAuth bearer errors from K8s Status responses.

Sources: RFC 6750 (2; 3; 5); RFC 7662 (2; 4); RFC 9700 / BCP 240 (2; 4.10; 4.14); RFC 7519 (3; 4.1; 5; 7; 11)

K8S01 — Human OIDC login to kubectl API read

Show the complete client login, token authentication and authorized Kubernetes read.

Actors: Alice; kubectl/client-go; Exec plugin + browser; OIDC issuer; API server; RBAC; Storage

Preconditions

  • Pinned cluster fixture; exec credential API client.authentication.k8s.io/v1; public native OIDC client kubernetes-demo; authorization code + S256 PKCE; Alice sub alice and group readers.
  1. login: kubectl calls exec plugin; plugin opens system browser at issuer and validates returned state; redeems code with verifier; validates ID token/nonce. Held state: Plugin owns PKCE verifier/state/nonce; issuer credentials stay at issuer; refresh token remains plugin-local.
  2. credential: Plugin returns ExecCredential status.token and expirationTimestamp. Held state: kubectl obtains ID token only; API server never receives refresh token, code or PKCE verifier.
  3. authenticate: kubectl sends Authorization: Bearer ID-token over TLS; API validates configured issuer/key/audience/expiry and maps identity. Held state: API request userInfo appears only after validation; no browser redirect originates at API server.
  4. authorize: GET /api/v1/namespaces/demo-dev/pods becomes list/core/pods/demo-dev; reader binding permits Alice. Held state: Local RBAC decision records matched subject, binding and rule.
  5. respond: Read storage through API server and return PodList; mark admission not applicable to reads. Held state: Result bytes reach kubectl; token validity has not granted blanket access.

Negative cases

  • Wrong PKCE verifier/state/nonce stops client login.
  • No matching reader binding yields 403 after successful authentication.

Acceptance

  • A cache-hit second request has no interactive login or per-request issuer introspection.
  • No API-server password form, automatic browser launch, or implicit Kubernetes User object creation.

Sources: OpenID Connect Core 1.0, errata set 2 (2; 3.1.2; 3.1.3.7; 12; 16.15); RFC 7636 (4); RFC 8252 (7; 8); Kubernetes Authenticating: user-requested OIDC source (OIDC tokens; structured configuration; client-go credential plugins; anonymous requests); Kubernetes Client Authentication v1 API (ExecCredentialSpec and ExecCredentialStatus); Kubernetes Controlling Access to the API (Authentication; authorization; admission)

K8S02 — JWT claims to Kubernetes userInfo

Make username and group mapping inspectable before access decisions.

Actors: OIDC issuer; API JWT authenticator; Alice/Bob; SelfSubjectReview

Preconditions

  • Structured AuthenticationConfiguration v1; username claim sub with prefix oidc:; groups claim groups with prefix team:; required tenant demo; reject mapped system: names.
  1. validate: Accept issuer/audience/cryptographic and configured tenant claims. Held state: Validated token is distinct from its mapped Kubernetes identity.
  2. map: Map alice to oidc:alice and readers to team:readers; add normal authenticated group. Held state: API builds userInfo; no role or RoleBinding is created from a group claim.
  3. inspect: Run kubectl auth whoami / SelfSubjectReview. Held state: Response identifies caller mapping; no persisted User or review object.
  4. contrast: Map Bob with observers and attempt same pod read. Held state: Bob authenticates but lacks reader binding; authorization is still separate.

Negative cases

  • Missing/wrong-type required mapping claim or failed CEL validation fails authentication.
  • Unprefixed group/string mismatch gives no binding match; prefix collisions must not confer system identity.

Acceptance

  • Mapping table shows raw claim, configuration, mapped value and provenance.
  • Email variant must check email_verified; do not use mutable email as the default fixture key.

Sources: Kubernetes Authenticating: user-requested OIDC source (OIDC tokens; structured configuration; client-go credential plugins; anonymous requests); Kubernetes kube-apiserver configuration v1 (AuthenticationConfiguration; JWTAuthenticator; Issuer; ClaimMappings; UserValidationRule); kubectl auth whoami (SelfSubjectReview); Kubernetes RBAC Good Practices (Least privilege; escalation risks; user identity reuse)

K8S03 — Kubernetes JWT rejection and key rotation

Keep failed credential validation outside RBAC and admission.

Actors: kubectl; API JWT authenticator; Issuer metadata/JWKS cache

Preconditions

  • OIDC ID-token profile audience kubernetes-demo; RS256 fixtures; unknown-key refresh semantics labeled as implementation-specific; link JWT04-JWT07.
  1. receive: Receive a bearer token for a pod request. Held state: Token bytes initially untrusted; no request userInfo.
  2. verify: Evaluate configured issuer discovery, key/signature, audience, expiry and claim/user validation. Held state: Record first rejecting check without exposing token secrets in logs.
  3. rotate: Use old/new issuer keys to exercise cache hit and unknown-kid refresh. Held state: No accepted identity until key resolution and verification succeed.
  4. reject: Return Kubernetes 401 Status for an invalid presented bearer credential in this isolated authenticator fixture. Held state: No RBAC decision, admission decision or storage write follows.

Negative cases

  • Bad signature, expired token, wrong audience, issuer mismatch and unknown key each get their own branch.
  • Discovery/JWKS outage is not proof of token invalidity; label infrastructure vs validation failure while denying unauthenticated access.

Acceptance

  • No silent conversion of invalid bearer to anonymous.
  • Do not invent AuthenticationConfiguration algorithm-list fields or combine --authentication-config with --oidc-*; optional flag-only comparison explicitly sets --oidc-signing-algs=RS256.

Sources: Kubernetes Authenticating: user-requested OIDC source (OIDC tokens; structured configuration; client-go credential plugins; anonymous requests); Kubernetes kube-apiserver configuration v1 (AuthenticationConfiguration; JWTAuthenticator; Issuer; ClaimMappings; UserValidationRule); OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0, errata set 2 (3; 4.3; 7); RFC 8725 / BCP 225 (2; 3.1-3.12)

K8S04 — RoleBinding explains Alice allowed and Bob forbidden

Make one concrete namespaced permission decision fully traceable.

Actors: Alice; Bob; API server; RBAC rule store

Preconditions

  • demo-dev Role reader: core pods get/list/watch; RoleBinding read-pods subjects Group team:readers; Alice member, Bob not.
  1. authenticate: Accept either user token and show exact userInfo. Held state: Valid identities persist only for the corresponding request.
  2. attributes: Extract list/core/pods/namespace demo-dev from the request. Held state: Request attributes are explicit immutable input to authorization.
  3. match: Resolve binding subjects then roleRef then rule. Held state: Alice has matching path; Bob has none in the base demo chain (Node has no opinion for these non-node callers).
  4. result: Return PodList for Alice or 403 Forbidden for Bob. Held state: Bob remains authenticated; no login retry, admission or protected data result.

Negative cases

  • Change namespace to demo-prod or verb to delete: Alice denied.
  • A groups value named reader without an exact binding grants nothing.

Acceptance

  • Inspector displays subject → binding → role → matching rule → verdict.
  • Permission denial never alters or invents the JWT group claims.

Sources: Kubernetes Using RBAC Authorization (Roles/bindings; subjects; resource names; additive permissions; bind/escalate prevention); Kubernetes Authorization (Request attributes; verdicts; authorizer chain; access reviews)

K8S05 — Role and ClusterRole binding scope

Explain reusable rules versus the scope at which a binding grants them.

Actors: Alice; Bob; API server; RBAC

Preconditions

  • Independent resettable variants; custom demo-pod-reader ClusterRole; no built-in cluster-admin.
  1. namespace: Bind demo-pod-reader with a RoleBinding in demo-dev for Bob. Held state: Bob gains pod-read scope only in that namespace.
  2. compare: Request demo-prod pods and cluster nodes. Held state: Namespaced binding does not grant these requests.
  3. cluster: Separate fixture uses ClusterRoleBinding to grant same pod rules across namespaces. Held state: Both namespaces match; node access still absent because resource rule is pods.
  4. node: Separate demo-node-reader ClusterRole permits only get of named demo-node via ClusterRoleBinding. Held state: Cluster-scoped resource has no namespace attribute.

Negative cases

  • ClusterRole existence without any binding grants nothing.
  • RoleBinding roleRef Role from another namespace is not a valid cross-namespace grant; roleRef mutation is not a shortcut.

Acceptance

  • Four object kinds have a visible scope comparison; bindings contain subjects, roles contain rules.
  • Each variant resets policy state, so grants from previous variants cannot contaminate results.

Sources: Kubernetes Using RBAC Authorization (Roles/bindings; subjects; resource names; additive permissions; bind/escalate prevention); Kubernetes Authorization (Request attributes; verdicts; authorizer chain; access reviews)

K8S06 — Request attributes, subresources and can-i

Explain how an HTTP request becomes a policy question.

Actors: kubectl; API request parser; Authorization reviewer; RBAC

Preconditions

  • reader role; optional isolated get pods/log grant; named configmap demo-config rule; no wildcard resources.
  1. parse: Compare collection GET, named GET and GET pods/demo-pod/log. Held state: Derive list vs get, core group, namespace, name and log subresource.
  2. match: Evaluate pods separately from pods/log; evaluate resourceNames only for the named get fixture. Held state: Evidence records all compared fields; do not infer pod log rights from pod read.
  3. review: kubectl auth can-i creates SelfSubjectAccessReview for exact attributes. Held state: Review result is advisory at that evaluation time, not a reusable grant or admission success.
  4. execute: Issue actual request and evaluate current policy again. Held state: Reads skip admission; successful response requires current authorization.

Negative cases

  • Adding a namespace flag cannot turn a cluster-scoped resource into namespaced scope.
  • Do not present resourceNames as a filter on an unrestricted list; a list/watch variant needs the appropriate name field selector and checked semantics.

Acceptance

  • Explain core apiGroup as empty string, and distinguish API verbs from HTTP methods.
  • Show non-resource path example separately with lower-case HTTP verb; do not manufacture resource fields.

Sources: Kubernetes Authorization (Request attributes; verdicts; authorizer chain; access reviews); Kubernetes Using RBAC Authorization (Roles/bindings; subjects; resource names; additive permissions; bind/escalate prevention); kubectl auth can-i (Request checks; subresources; impersonation); Kubernetes SubjectAccessReview v1 API (ResourceAttributes and NonResourceAttributes; status)

K8S07 — Additive RBAC and group binding union

Prevent deny-rule and automatic-role misconceptions.

Actors: Bob; API server; RBAC bindings

Preconditions

  • Two custom bindings: readers gives pod reads; log-readers gives pod log get; separate group claims fixture.
  1. identify: Validate Bob group membership in both configured groups. Held state: Identity is accepted independently of permission computation.
  2. union: Gather matching RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding grants applicable to request scope. Held state: Display contributing rules; there is no RBAC deny rule overriding another grant.
  3. allow: Allow a request when at least one applicable matching rule grants it. Held state: Store matched-grant explanation, not a guessed generic role label.
  4. deny: For secrets get, no rule matches; all demo authorizers have no opinion and overall request is denied. Held state: Return 403; retain no secret data.

Negative cases

  • Removing one grant does not remove access still granted by another binding.
  • A nonmatching restrictive-looking role does not subtract permissions; a JWT group alone grants none.

Acceptance

  • Keep RBAC additive union distinct from sequential multi-authorizer chain semantics in K8S16.
  • system:authenticated is membership, not automatic admin permission.

Sources: Kubernetes Using RBAC Authorization (Roles/bindings; subjects; resource names; additive permissions; bind/escalate prevention); Kubernetes Authorization (Request attributes; verdicts; authorizer chain; access reviews)

K8S08 — Authorized writes, admission and persistence

Show authorization success that still fails admission, and the path to storage when admitted.

Actors: Alice writer fixture; API server; Mutating admission; Validating admission; Storage

Preconditions

  • Separate demo-writer role allows create configmaps in demo-dev; custom validation requires label training=approved; no actual production resources.
  1. authorize: Authenticate Alice and authorize create/core/configmaps/demo-dev. Held state: Request identity and authorization verdict exist; storage unchanged.
  2. mutate: Run mutating admission phase; the core fixture has no matching custom mutation. An optional annotation webhook can show mutation separately. Held state: Original proposal remains unchanged in core; an optional modified proposal gets a new representation and provenance.
  3. validate: Validate the proposed object against explicit label policy. Held state: Admission rejection leaves no persisted ConfigMap; rejection reason identifies admission rather than RBAC.
  4. persist: For accepted fixture, complete API validation and persist, then return 201 with server-assigned metadata. Held state: Stored object is distinct from request and admission proposal; read-back shows persisted bytes.

Negative cases

  • Missing label fails admission despite RBAC allow.
  • Invalid object schema or storage conflict has its own failure origin; do not label every non-401 as RBAC failure.

Acceptance

  • GET/list/watch comparison bypasses admission.
  • Use a checked API status fixture; do not hardcode one universal HTTP error code for all admission policies.

Sources: Kubernetes Controlling Access to the API (Authentication; authorization; admission); Kubernetes Admission Control (What are they?; mutating and validating phases; read bypass); Kubernetes Validating Admission Policy (Stable v1.30; matchConstraints; validations; binding validationActions); Kubernetes Dynamic Admission Control (AdmissionReview; matching; failure policy; alpha webhook-token feature)

K8S09 — Projected ServiceAccount token issuance and rotation

Show workload credentials as Kubernetes-issued bound tokens.

Actors: ServiceAccount reader; Pod demo-reader; Kubelet; API TokenRequest issuer; Workload

Preconditions

  • Namespace demo-dev; Pod UID pod-1; ServiceAccount UID sa-1; projected token volume; audience https://kubernetes.demo.example; requested lifetime 3600s but returned expiry authoritative.
  1. request: Authorized kubelet requests token for reader, audience and Pod binding. Held state: Kubelet has node credential; API signer key stays in issuer boundary; workload does not choose arbitrary identity.
  2. issue: API issues signed JWT with subject, issuer, audiences, lifetime and binding identifiers. Held state: TokenRequest response carries token; no automatic token Secret created.
  3. project: Kubelet writes projection; workload reads token file and calls API over TLS. Held state: Workload acquires token only when reading projection; file presence alone is not API acceptance.
  4. rotate: Kubelet requests replacement and updates projected content; app reloads token. Held state: Old/new generation and expiry remain distinct; replacement does not instantly revoke a still-valid old generation.

Negative cases

  • Cached old bytes eventually expire; file update does not magically update application memory.
  • automountServiceAccountToken false prevents automatic mount, not all possible manually configured credential issuance.

Acceptance

  • Show rotation trigger as documented 80% TTL or 24h, while respecting returned expiry and selected server extension settings.
  • Default lesson is projected bounded token, not manually created long-lived service-account-token Secret.

Sources: Kubernetes Service Accounts (TokenRequest; permissions; authenticating service account credentials); Kubernetes Configure Service Accounts for Pods (Projection; issuer/audience flags; token rotation); Kubernetes Managing Service Accounts (Bound token lifetime; private claims; TokenReview versus offline verification)

K8S10 — ServiceAccount identities and RBAC subjects

Explain workload group membership and why token possession does not grant namespace access.

Actors: Pod reader; API ServiceAccount authenticator; RBAC

Preconditions

  • reader ServiceAccount in demo-dev; bound token from K8S09; no default resource permissions beyond declared cluster defaults.
  1. authenticate: Validate service-account token and current binding objects. Held state: Map system:serviceaccount:demo-dev:reader with groups system:serviceaccounts, system:serviceaccounts:demo-dev and system:authenticated.
  2. deny: Before fixture binding, request demo-dev pods. Held state: No matching grant; return 403 after successful authentication.
  3. bind: Resettable fixture adds RoleBinding subject kind ServiceAccount, name reader, namespace demo-dev to Role reader. Held state: Explicit grant path now matches this workload.
  4. group: Compare separate group binding for system:serviceaccounts:demo-dev versus global system:serviceaccounts. Held state: Highlight subject scope expansion without granting cluster-admin or wildcard resources.

Negative cases

  • Same ServiceAccount name in demo-prod is a different principal.
  • ServiceAccount namespace does not automatically restrict every permission it could be granted elsewhere.

Acceptance

  • Distinguish singular system:serviceaccount username prefix from plural group prefix.
  • No generic human OIDC group can become a ServiceAccount merely by copying a string; enforce configured human mapping boundaries.

Sources: Kubernetes Service Accounts (TokenRequest; permissions; authenticating service account credentials); Kubernetes Using RBAC Authorization (Roles/bindings; subjects; resource names; additive permissions; bind/escalate prevention); Kubernetes Managing Service Accounts (Bound token lifetime; private claims; TokenReview versus offline verification)

K8S11 — TokenReview versus offline service-account JWT validation

Compare current bound-object checks with offline cryptographic validation.

Actors: Workload token holder; External resource service; API TokenReview; Offline validator; Cluster object store

Preconditions

  • External service has its own credential permitting create tokenreviews; presented token audience vault.demo.example; object-bound token not yet expired.
  1. submit: External service calls TokenReview using its own reviewer credential, with presented token in spec.token and expected audience in spec.audiences. Held state: Reviewer credential and reviewed token are distinct artifacts.
  2. review: API checks token plus ServiceAccount/Pod UID and existence; service checks authenticated and matching status.audiences. Held state: Successful review authenticates token subject; no resource permission is granted by this response.
  3. offline: Compare separate validator using trusted cluster discovery/JWKS, signature and issuer/audience/time. Held state: It cannot learn current Pod deletion from signed claims alone.
  4. delete: Delete Pod or change UID; replay token in both paths before exp. Held state: Live review rejects after documented lifecycle rules; offline path may remain valid until expiry without extra online checks.

Negative cases

  • authenticated=true with no expected returned audience is insufficient for a custom audience.
  • Pending deletion has documented 60s threshold; do not promise all deletions invalidate every validator instantly.

Acceptance

  • TokenReview itself is not stored in etcd.
  • External service performs its own authorization after authentication; local JWT validation is not an OIDC browser login.

Sources: Kubernetes TokenReview v1 API (TokenReviewSpec and TokenReviewStatus audiences/authenticated/user); Kubernetes Managing Service Accounts (Bound token lifetime; private claims; TokenReview versus offline verification); Kubernetes Service Accounts (TokenRequest; permissions; authenticating service account credentials)

K8S12 — Audience-isolated ServiceAccount TokenRequest

Show Kubernetes issuer versus human issuer, and target-specific workload credentials.

Actors: Pod; Kubelet/API TokenRequest; Kubernetes API; External vault fixture

Preconditions

  • Two separate projected tokens for same ServiceAccount: Kubernetes API audience and vault.demo.example; cluster issuer distinct from external human issuer.
  1. issue: Request each intended audience through an authorized TokenRequest path. Held state: Separate exact token artifacts with returned expiry and issuer.
  2. api: Present API-audience token to Kubernetes; validate ServiceAccount path and RBAC. Held state: No human OIDC claim mapping is reused.
  3. vault: Present vault-audience token to external service; use K8S11 review/local configured validation and external policy. Held state: Vault retains only its accepted identity/decision, not a Kubernetes RoleBinding.
  4. swap: Send either token to the unintended audience. Held state: Audience rejection prevents cross-service acceptance.

Negative cases

  • TokenRequest is not unauthenticated token minting; unauthorized callers cannot choose arbitrary ServiceAccounts.
  • Kubernetes discovery/JWKS publishing does not make ServiceAccount issuer a full interactive OIDC login provider.

Acceptance

  • Display authentication issuer, token audience, resource endpoint and policy authority separately.
  • Do not claim token expiry always equals requested expirationSeconds; use returned status.expirationTimestamp.

Sources: Kubernetes Service Accounts (TokenRequest; permissions; authenticating service account credentials); Kubernetes Configure Service Accounts for Pods (Projection; issuer/audience flags; token rotation); Kubernetes TokenReview v1 API (TokenReviewSpec and TokenReviewStatus audiences/authenticated/user); Kubernetes Managing Service Accounts (Bound token lifetime; private claims; TokenReview versus offline verification)

K8S13 — Missing credentials, anonymous identity and 401/403

Avoid a misleading universal status-code shortcut.

Actors: Unauthenticated client; API authenticators; Anonymous authenticator; RBAC

Preconditions

  • Isolated variants: anonymous disabled; anonymous allowed only /livez; separately full anonymous with no pod permission.
  1. missing: Request pods without credentials when anonymous disabled. Held state: No identity accepted; return 401 in selected fixture.
  2. invalid: Present invalid bearer with anonymous enabled. Held state: Credential rejection remains 401; no fallback anonymous identity.
  3. anonymous: Send no credential to permitted anonymous endpoint. Held state: Map system:anonymous/system:unauthenticated; authorization still evaluates route permission.
  4. forbidden: In full-anonymous comparison, request pods with no matching grant. Held state: Anonymous identity exists but RBAC rejects: 403; endpoint-only mode blocks unsupported anonymous paths earlier.

Negative cases

  • Do not state all missing credentials always yield 401 or all 403 imply authenticated human.
  • Path allowlisting for anonymous authentication is not itself an RBAC permission grant.

Acceptance

  • Display failing stage and identity alongside response code.
  • Use stable AuthenticationConfiguration anonymous fields; do not combine anonymous config with --anonymous-auth flag.

Sources: Kubernetes Authenticating: user-requested OIDC source (OIDC tokens; structured configuration; client-go credential plugins; anonymous requests); Kubernetes kube-apiserver configuration v1 (AuthenticationConfiguration; JWTAuthenticator; Issuer; ClaimMappings; UserValidationRule); Kubernetes Authorization (Request attributes; verdicts; authorizer chain; access reviews)

K8S14 — Impersonation permission and constrained variant

Explain original caller, impersonated identity and the extra authorization checks.

Actors: Demo operator; API authentication/impersonation; Target oidc:bob; RBAC; Audit

Preconditions

  • Classic variant permits only target oidc:bob via explicit impersonate resourceNames; target gets reader through fixture. Separate constrained variant beta since 1.36 with gate state shown.
  1. caller: Authenticate original operator before processing Impersonate-User. Held state: Audit retains original authenticated identity; header alone grants nothing.
  2. check: Authorize every requested impersonation attribute; classic target restriction is identity restriction, not action/namespace confinement. Held state: Reject unauthorized user/group/extra header; no forged accepted identity.
  3. target: Evaluate actual pod request with permitted impersonated userInfo. Held state: Show impersonated identity and target authorization result; original permissions are not simply unioned in.
  4. constrain: In separate beta fixture, require identity permission plus impersonate-on:user-info:list in demo-dev, with no legacy impersonate fallback grant. Held state: Permit listed action only when all applicable checks pass; preserve original/impersonated audit provenance.

Negative cases

  • Constrained identity permission without action permission fails.
  • If legacy impersonate is also granted, failed constrained check may fall back; show why that fixture is not confined.

Acceptance

  • Version/gate badge visible; no unlabelled assertion of stable constrained impersonation.
  • Keep scope to demo users; no node impersonation or system:masters example.

Sources: Kubernetes User Impersonation (Classic impersonation; constrained impersonation beta; fallback; auditing); Kubernetes Authorization (Request attributes; verdicts; authorizer chain; access reviews); Kubernetes RBAC Good Practices (Least privilege; escalation risks; user identity reuse)

K8S15 — Role creation, bind and escalate safeguards

Explain why CRUD rights on RBAC objects alone cannot delegate arbitrary power.

Actors: Limited policy editor; API RBAC REST validation; RBAC rule store

Preconditions

  • Separate nonproduction editor can create roles/rolebindings in demo-dev; owns pod-read rights; no bind or escalate permission initially.
  1. role: Attempt to create role granting secrets read which editor lacks. Held state: Ordinary create authorization may pass; escalation prevention rejects; stored RBAC unchanged.
  2. binding: Attempt to bind a role exceeding current permissions. Held state: Bind restriction independently rejects; a new permission grant is not persisted.
  3. allowed: Create/bind only pod-reader rights already held at scope. Held state: After checks, persisted binding can affect later requests.
  4. delegate: Show separate tightly scoped bind permission for one custom role; describe escalate as separate explicit privilege. Held state: State reset and limited roleRef prevent accidental broad grants.

Negative cases

  • Having create rolebindings does not by itself permit binding cluster-admin.
  • Namespace editor cannot grant cluster-wide privileges via RoleBinding.

Acceptance

  • Name bind/escalate checks separately from ordinary request authorization and admission.
  • No default demo manifest grants wildcard bind/escalate or system:masters.

Sources: Kubernetes Using RBAC Authorization (Roles/bindings; subjects; resource names; additive permissions; bind/escalate prevention); Kubernetes RBAC Good Practices (Least privilege; escalation risks; user identity reuse); Kubernetes Authorization (Request attributes; verdicts; authorizer chain; access reviews)

K8S16 — Optional authentication and authorization webhooks (optional extension)

Keep three different extension interfaces distinct.

Actors: Bearer client; API server; Token authentication webhook; Authorization webhook; Admission webhook

Preconditions

  • Optional clearly labeled extensions; explicit authentication.k8s.io/v1 TokenReview and authorization.k8s.io/v1 SubjectAccessReview; authenticated TLS transport; chosen cache/timeout/failure policies visible.
  1. authenticate: For an opaque bearer fixture, API calls token-authentication webhook with TokenReview and obtains userInfo. Held state: Remote result accepted only after transport/response validation; no access grant yet.
  2. authorize: Build request attributes; evaluate explicitly ordered authorizer chain and call authorization webhook if reached. Held state: SubjectAccessReview allowed/denied/no-opinion belongs to request decision, not identity validation.
  3. order: Compare Webhook-before-RBAC versus RBAC-before-Webhook with explicit allow/deny fixture. Held state: First decisive authorizer ends chain; all no opinion means deny; RBAC union rule is not the whole-chain rule.
  4. admit: For allowed write, optional AdmissionReview is a separate post-authorization interface. Held state: No TokenReview or SubjectAccessReview artifact is reused as admission approval.

Negative cases

  • Webhook outage follows chosen failure policy/cache; do not invent one universal response.
  • Earlier RBAC allow can bypass later authorization webhook; label this operational consequence.

Acceptance

  • This is not the default OIDC path; no forced per-request issuer TokenReview.
  • Do not enable the v1.37 alpha admission-webhook token authentication feature as an unlabeled default.

Sources: Kubernetes Authenticating: user-requested OIDC source (OIDC tokens; structured configuration; client-go credential plugins; anonymous requests); Kubernetes Authorization Webhook Mode (SubjectAccessReview request/response and caching); Kubernetes Authorization (Request attributes; verdicts; authorizer chain; access reviews); Kubernetes Dynamic Admission Control (AdmissionReview; matching; failure policy; alpha webhook-token feature); Kubernetes TokenReview v1 API (TokenReviewSpec and TokenReviewStatus audiences/authenticated/user)

Exact manifest and configuration bundles

Do not apply all bundles together. Core and per-scenario extensions are separate; isolated variants start from a reset fixture. Values with ${...} are explicitly runtime substitutions. JSON objects are exact manifest bodies, also valid YAML. These plan fixtures have not been live-applied.

Install only for admission scenario. Core mutating phase is a no-op. Submit each ConfigMap as a separate request; the rejected proposal must never be persisted.

{
  "id": "admission-write",
  "classification": "core scenario extension",
  "scenarioIds": [
    "K8S08"
  ],
  "instructions": "Install only for admission scenario. Core mutating phase is a no-op. Submit each ConfigMap as a separate request; the rejected proposal must never be persisted.",
  "objects": [
    {
      "apiVersion": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1",
      "kind": "Role",
      "metadata": {
        "name": "demo-writer",
        "namespace": "demo-dev"
      },
      "rules": [
        {
          "apiGroups": [
            ""
          ],
          "resources": [
            "configmaps"
          ],
          "verbs": [
            "create",
            "get"
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "apiVersion": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1",
      "kind": "RoleBinding",
      "metadata": {
        "name": "alice-demo-writer",
        "namespace": "demo-dev"
      },
      "subjects": [
        {
          "kind": "User",
          "name": "oidc:alice",
          "apiGroup": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
        }
      ],

        "apiGroup": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io",
        "kind": "Role",
        "name": "demo-writer"
      }
    },
    {
      "apiVersion": "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1",
      "kind": "ValidatingAdmissionPolicy",
      "metadata": {
        "name": "demo-training-label"
      },
      "spec": {
        "failurePolicy": "Fail",
        "matchConstraints": {
          "resourceRules": [
            {
              "apiGroups": [
                ""
              ],
              "apiVersions": [
                "v1"
              ],
              "operations": [
                "CREATE"
              ],
              "resources": [
                "configmaps"
              ],
              "scope": "Namespaced"
            }
          ]
        },
        "validations": [
          {
            "expression": "has(object.metadata.labels) && 'training' in object.metadata.labels && object.metadata.labels['training'] == 'approved'",
            "message": "demo ConfigMaps require training=approved"
          }
        ]
      }
    },
    {
      "apiVersion": "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1",
      "kind": "ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding",
      "metadata": {
        "name": "demo-training-label"
      },
      "spec": {
        "policyName": "demo-training-label",
        "validationActions": [
          "Deny"
        ],
        "matchResources": {
          "namespaceSelector": {
            "matchLabels": {
              "authflow.example/fixture": "true"
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

projected-workload — core scenario extension — K8S09, K8S12

Worker builds the local demo reader image and pins its digest for any live run. The example is deliberately not a downloadable third-party workload. Explicit projection still works with automatic mounting disabled. For API TLS, provide trusted CA separately; never skip server verification.

{
  "id": "projected-workload",
  "classification": "core scenario extension",
  "scenarioIds": [
    "K8S09",
    "K8S12"
  ],
  "instructions": "Worker builds the local demo reader image and pins its digest for any live run. The example is deliberately not a downloadable third-party workload. Explicit projection still works with automatic mounting disabled. For API TLS, provide trusted CA separately; never skip server verification.",
  "objects": [
    {
      "apiVersion": "v1",
      "kind": "Pod",
      "metadata": {
        "name": "demo-reader",
        "namespace": "demo-dev"
      },
      "spec": {
        "serviceAccountName": "reader",
        "automountServiceAccountToken": false,
        "containers": [
          {
            "name": "reader",
            "image": "authflow-reader:local",
            "imagePullPolicy": "Never",
            "volumeMounts": [
              {
                "name": "identity",
                "mountPath": "/var/run/demo-identity",
                "readOnly": true
              }
            ]
          }
        ],
        "volumes": [
          {
            "name": "identity",
            "projected": {
              "sources": [
                {
                  "serviceAccountToken": {
                    "path": "api-token",
                    "audience": "https://kubernetes.demo.example",
                    "expirationSeconds": 3600
                  }
                },
                {
                  "serviceAccountToken": {
                    "path": "vault-token",
                    "audience": "vault.demo.example",
                    "expirationSeconds": 3600
                  }
                }
              ]
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}

token-request-and-review — request templates — K8S11, K8S12

Substitute observed UID and exact issued token; templates are not ready-to-send credentials. TokenRequest POST /api/v1/namespaces/demo-dev/serviceaccounts/reader/token; TokenReview POST /apis/authentication.k8s.io/v1/tokenreviews. Authorization header on review uses the reviewer credential, not spec.token.

{
  "id": "token-request-and-review",
  "classification": "request templates",
  "scenarioIds": [
    "K8S11",
    "K8S12"
  ],
  "instructions": "Substitute observed UID and exact issued token; templates are not ready-to-send credentials. TokenRequest POST /api/v1/namespaces/demo-dev/serviceaccounts/reader/token; TokenReview POST /apis/authentication.k8s.io/v1/tokenreviews. Authorization header on review uses the reviewer credential, not spec.token.",
  "objects": [
    {
      "apiVersion": "authentication.k8s.io/v1",
      "kind": "TokenRequest",
      "spec": {
        "audiences": [
          "vault.demo.example"
        ],
        "expirationSeconds": 3600,
        "boundObjectRef": {
          "kind": "Pod",
          "apiVersion": "v1",
          "name": "demo-reader",
          "uid": "${OBSERVED_POD_UID}"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "apiVersion": "authentication.k8s.io/v1",
      "kind": "TokenReview",
      "spec": {
        "token": "${PRESENTED_VAULT_TOKEN}",
        "audiences": [
          "vault.demo.example"
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}

core-api-configuration — core — K8S01, K8S02, K8S09

Partial API-server security configuration, not a complete cluster bootstrap command. Add independently provisioned TLS, etcd and node credentials. Signing private key remains server-local. No --oidc-* or --anonymous-auth flags with this authentication file; no --authorization-mode with this authorization file.

{
  "id": "core-api-configuration",
  "classification": "core",
  "scenarioIds": [
    "K8S01",
    "K8S02",
    "K8S09"
  ],
  "configurationFiles": {
    "authentication.yaml": {
      "apiVersion": "apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1",
      "kind": "AuthenticationConfiguration",
      "anonymous": {
        "enabled": false
      },
      "jwt": [
        {
          "issuer": {
            "url": "https://issuer.demo.example",
            "audiences": [
              "kubernetes-demo"
            ],
            "audienceMatchPolicy": "MatchAny"
          },
          "claimValidationRules": [
            {
              "claim": "tenant",
              "requiredValue": "demo"
            }
          ],
          "claimMappings": {
            "username": {
              "claim": "sub",
              "prefix": "oidc:"
            },
            "groups": {
              "claim": "groups",
              "prefix": "team:"
            }
          },
          "userValidationRules": [
            {
              "expression": "!user.username.startsWith('system:')",
              "message": "human username must not use a system prefix"
            },
            {
              "expression": "user.groups.all(group, !group.startsWith('system:'))",
              "message": "mapped human groups must not use a system prefix"
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    "authorization.yaml": {
      "apiVersion": "apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1",
      "kind": "AuthorizationConfiguration",
      "authorizers": [
        {
          "type": "Node",
          "name": "node"
        },
        {
          "type": "RBAC",
          "name": "rbac"
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "arguments": [
    "--authentication-config=/etc/demo/authentication.yaml",
    "--authorization-config=/etc/demo/authorization.yaml",
    "--service-account-issuer=https://kubernetes.demo.example",
    "--api-audiences=https://kubernetes.demo.example",
    "--service-account-signing-key-file=/etc/demo/sa-signing.key",
    "--service-account-key-file=/etc/demo/sa-verification.pub",
    "--service-account-extend-token-expiration=false"
  ],
  "instructions": "Partial API-server security configuration, not a complete cluster bootstrap command. Add independently provisioned TLS, etcd and node credentials. Signing private key remains server-local. No --oidc-* or --anonymous-auth flags with this authentication file; no --authorization-mode with this authorization file."
}
